This misconception which was afforded by the speech of the Minister of Agriculture has been repeated in the province of Ontario and undoubtedly it will be hard to catch up with. I propose for a few moments this afternoon to deal at least in part with this particular aspect of the problem that concerns us at the present time. The fact is that the farmers of Canada are not as well off today as the Minister of Agriculture sought to portray. I note that when he spoke in Saskatoon the other day he presented a picture of moderate optimism as to the outlook for agriculture on the prairies. He did not give that impression in the house when he spoke in introducing his estimates. He argued that there had been a rise in the net agricultural income across the board. He did not differentiate between one section of Canada and another. I am sure, for instance, that when he made that speech he did not take into account the summary of statistics, dated February, 1961, presented to the standing committee on agriculture and colonization by an official of his department. On page 7 of the report, which was prepared by Mr. Gordon Haase, the following is to be noted:
The behaviour of certain farm prices was examined . . . and the results of these price movements can be interpreted in terms of their final effects upon total farm income and expenses.
At the conclusion on page 8 the author observes:
It should also be noted that this changing relationship of farm income and expense has had different effects in each province reflecting the particular types of farming that are practised.
In examining the minister's statement I think it is important that we bear in mind certain facts and among them is the fact that Canada's gross national product in current dollars increased from $16.3 billion in 1949 to $34.6 billion in 1959 and to an estimated $35.5 billion or thereabouts in 1960. With this as a background I should like to observe that while productivity in agriculture has risen rapidly, prices for farm products have not increased in step with increased costs. The report prepared by Mr. Haase for the standing committee on agriculture, and it is well worth examining, clearly establishes this fact. I think we have to examine the problem facing the farmers of our country with the background of present economic conditions in Canada. I cannot believe that any occupational group in any section of Canada can be well off for very long when the general level of economic activity is declining; when there is very serious unemployment and so long as our basic financial monetary exchange, trade and commercial policies are the subject of much criticism throughout the country.

Supp ly-A griculture
Although changes in agricultural conditions are inevitable, we must be sure that the major changes are not brought about too quickly at a time when unemployment, as at present, is at an unprecedentedly high level. We must realize that there are some social problems facing the farmers which must be solved with sympathy and understanding.
The agricultural revolution of today places many farm people in a comparable position to that brought about by the industrial revolution of the last century. Rather than have these people leave the farms, as some suggest, and move to urban areas where they would add to the numbers of unemployed, it is preferable that they stay on the farms until employment opportunities in the cities increase. That puts a responsibility on the Canadian people as a whole, on this government and on this parliament.
As I see it, it is the responsibility of all Canadians to assure farmers a decent standard of living, and the measures taken toward this goal will be less expensive for the Canadian taxpayer in the long run than having to provide financial assistance to even greater numbers of unemployed people in Canada.
Dealing directly with the matter of the cash income of the Canadian farmer in 1960, I think it is important to bear in mind certain statistics that were not dealt with by the Minister of Agriculture. An examination of the statistics produced by his department through the economics research division of the Department of Agriculture reveals that the cash income from farm products declined in 1960 to $2,784 million, from $2,789 million in 1959, and $2,795 million in 1958. What the minister has done in the figures that he has given to the committee to show the alleged rise in net farm income has been to exclude from his calculations transfer payments that have been made under various measures passed in this house providing assistance in one form or another to the farmers of Canada.
Supplementary payments to farmers in 1960, it should not be forgotten, amounted to $77 million. These payments were made under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, western grain producers acreage plan, the federal-provincial emergency unthreshed grain assistance policy and other measures. In 1959 the total supplementary payments amounted to $22 million only, most of which was received under the provisions of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. So there has been an increase in 1960 of $55 million in transfer payments to the agricultural sector of the economy. These transfer payments, representing an increase of $55 million, were overlooked by the minister and must be

calculated in determining the net farm income position of the Canadian farmer. In spite of this increase of $55 million in supplementary payments, the realized gross income of farmers rose by only $53 million, from $3,155 million in 1959 to $3,209 million in 1960.
This means that if one discounts the increase in government transfer payments the farmers' gross income declined in 1960 and did not increase as the Minister of Agriculture suggested to this committee and to the people of Canada. This statement is borne out by the dominion bureau of statistics compilation which was given out recently, and particularly the table entitled, "Net Income of Farm Operators from Farming Operations, Canada, by Provinces". This covers such things as cash income from farm products, income in kind, supplementary payments, realized gross income, operating and depreciation charges, realized net income, value of inventory changes, total gross income, and total net income. Hon. members will find this table, which was distributed by the minister or by the Department of Agriculture, of great significance in this regard. For instance, I find in the third paragraph of the commentary attached to this table the following statement, which bears out what I have said about the relationship between transfer payments and the calculation of the net farm income in 1960.
Supplementary payments to farmers in western Canada in 1960 amounted to approximately 77 million dollars and included payments made under the provisions of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act-
And the various other measures which I have already cited. It goes on to state:
This is in contrast to 1959 when farmers received approximately 22 million dollars, most of which was received under the provisions of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act.
So, this fact alone puts the enthusiastic statement made by the Minister of Agriculture, whose enthusiasm sometimes permits him to run ahead of his judgment, in proper perspective.
This is not the only fact. Since operating expenses of farmers rose by some $13 million according to the table to which I have already made reference, from $1,880 million in 1959 to $1,893 million in 1960, realized net income rose by only $41 million or about four fifths of the increase in transfer payments to farmers.
Moreover, the table also indicates that inventories on farms increased by $36 million in 1960 as opposed to a decrease of $70 million in 1959. It is indicated that this was due to an increase in grain production over the preceding year and a continuing build-up

of Canada's cattle population. So between 1959 and 1960 inventories accounted for a change of some $106 million.
I draw from all these facts the following conclusion: The total net income in 1960 was approximately $1,352 million. In 1959 it stood at $1,206 million. This was an increase of only $146 million despite the fact that there was a $55 million increase in transfer payments and a change in inventories held on the farms which amounted to $106 million. These two factors would account for a change in the cash income of some $160 million. Despite these facts-and notwithstanding what the Minister of Agriculture said, and notwithstanding what the propaganda agencies of the Department of Agriculture indicated -the net income rose by less than $146 million so that the underlying economic position of the agricultural community, after allowing for an increase in transfer payments and a change in inventories, deteriorated in 1960.
That is in direct contradiction to what the Minister of Agriculture told this House of Commons. The government can take no credit for the increase in the yield of wheat or the continuing increase in the number of cattle which is the major factor in the change in the farmers' net income position. This was not the result of government policy. I am sure that even the Minister of Agriculture would say that these were factors that went far beyond the reach of government action. This government has nothing that warrants being called an agricultural policy. The increase in transfer payments which took place was the result of abnormal conditions that existed on the prairies during the last year; I refer, for instance, to such things as the early snowfall that caught the wheat unharvested in the fields.
Furthermore, a cursory look at the regional distribution of net income from farm operations reveals, I believe, a complete lack of a national agricultural policy. Yet I have in my hand here a document with a large blue streak across the top on a white background, addressed to certain people who are meeting in Ottawa at the present time for some undisclosed purpose. If one examines that document, one will find that this government has, according to its own impression, a clear-cut agricultural policy designed to meet not only the long term aspect of the problem but the short term aspect of it as well.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: That is a first-class document.

My hon. friend says it is a first-class document. He is right if one interprets that statement in the proper sense. It is a first-class Madison avenue product. That is what it is. All the propaganda
Supply-Agriculture
of the government engineered by the archpropagandist of the government, namely the Minister of Agriculture, is not going to convince the Canadian farmer that his position under this government is greatly improved over what it was when this government took office. The fact is that farm net income declined in British Columbia, Alberta, Manitoba and Quebec. The increase of over $100 million in Saskatchewan resulted from a good wheat crop and the increased transfer payments to western farmers. The increase in Ontario was largely accounted for by the increase in the inventory of cattle held on the farm. When the minister deals with the various submissions that have been made during the course of discussion on the first item, I hope he will address himself to the figures which I have produced and which come from his own publications. I challenge him now, in the face of these figures, to deny the picture which I have presented of the actual income position of the farmers of Canada at the present time.
The minister is a man of great enthusiasm and for that quality he is to be admired and congratulated. But when a man is administering a large department of government, he should not allow his enthusiasm in any way to discolour his judgment or to interfere with his capacity for good judgment. He must see things as they are and not as he would like them to be. A good case in point to illustrate what I have in mind is a statement made by the Minister of Agriculture two weeks ago when he said:
The action taken by the government last year in placing hog support on a deficiency payment basis has had the anticipated effect of eliminating the previous surplus production and greatly improving hog prices.
That was a statement by the Minister of of Agriculture. I do not think that statement can stand any test of real validity. However, the minister is entitled to make an argument. Nevertheless, I suggest that no department of the government of Canada is warranted in using its agencies for the purpose of spreading political propaganda.
Oh, oh.

I have before me the statement that came from the information division of the Canadian Department of Agriculture repeating precisely the words of the minister. I now quote what that information division says:
-the action taken by the government in placing hog support on a deficiency payment basis has had the anticipated effect of eliminating the previous surplus production and greatly improving hog prices.
That is a complete reproduction of a political statement that was made by the Minister

Supply-Agriculture
of Agriculture. The information division of that department or of any other department has no right to use its services, which are paid for by the taxpayers of Canada, in order to try to put forward the government's answer to suggestions made in the House of Commons concerning the application of aspects of its agricultural policy. Lest anyone think that I am giving an argument that is specious, I have before me the Farmer's Advocate of February 25, 1961. Here is what it says:
As you can see the two statements-
That is the one by the information division and the one by the Minister of Agriculture.
-are identical. Is the information division-
The editor asks this question.
-becoming an agency for repeating party propaganda? Surely the task of the information division is to inform not to repeat political overstatements.
And an overstatement it is.
So says the editor. He continues:
Anyone who believes hog prices are now high solely because of the new deficiency payment system of price support is living in his own little dream world. Deficiency payments for hogs were instituted mainly to get the government out of the hog business (their storages were full at the time).
The reason hog prices are good now is because a good many farmers have no hogs to sell. The reason they have no hogs to sell is because they lost their shirts when prices dipped so low a little more than a year ago.
No wonder the editor concludes his observations by saying this:
And let's keep politics out of the government Information bureau.
I now make this suggestion to the Minister of Agriculture. He is beginning the administration of an important department. We all wish him well in the discharge of that function. However, he will not do the cause of agriculture much good by failing to make a distinction between his functions as a politician and his functions as Minister of Agriculture.
He will never come up to your record.

I think that is true. The only difference between the Minister of Agriculture and me is that I am simply an ordinary private member of the House of Commons and the man to whom my remarks are addressed holds an extremely important post as a minister of the crown. He has been in that office only a short time and I believe he will be there for only a short time. Mr. Chairman, no one will deny that our country is faced with a recession. This we have been experiencing for a short time. Now this recession, which began in the second

quarter of 1960, is commencing to show its impact on prices received for farm products. The ability of our economy to recover is impeded by the level of the income earned in the farm sector. Thus, both the farm and the non-farm segments of our economy have a vested interest in seeing to it that farmers are better compensated than they are at the present time.
This government was going to remove the cost-price squeeze in which farmers find themselves. In fairness to the present minister I will say that he has not yet made the extravagant claim made by his predecessor, namely that the present administration had removed the difficulties of the cost-price squeeze. However, I suspect that one must not allow the Minister of Agriculture to fall into the same error as that into which his predecessor fell.
Let us look into this business of the cost-price squeeze, something which greatly concerns the farmers as we know from the representations made in the briefs presented to this government by the national farmers union and the federation of agriculture, and about which not one word was said by the Minister of Agriculture when he introduced his estimates a week or two ago. Some insight into the deterioration of the farmers' financial position can be gained by referring to the following statistics which I obtained from the minister's own figures. I refer, first of all, to the index number of farm prices for the three years 1958, 1959 and 1960. The index number of farm prices in 1958 was 245.5. In 1959, it was 243.1 and in 1960, 236.6. Comparing the figures for those three years with the prices of commodities and services used by farmers in the same period, including farm living costs, we find the following: 242.7, 249.8, 253.6. The result is that the index of farm prices declined by 3.6 per cent between 1958 and 1960 while, on the other hand, the price of commodities used by farmers increased by 4.5 per cent. This is what is meant when the farmer says he is caught in the cost-price squeeze.
The Minister of Agriculture must address himself to this aspect of our presentation because one of the contentions made by the government when it introduced the Agricultural Stabilization Act through the instrumentality of the former minister of agriculture, and one of the assurances given by members sitting on the treasury benches, was that they were going to eliminate this situation which confronts the Canadian farmers. The figures which I have just quoted fairly establish the extent to which the government has been able to meet this problem. In the light of this deterioration in the position of the Canadian farmer, what

should be the objectives of the federal government's agricultural policy? I ask the minister that question.
In his speech in Saskatoon the other day he told the Saskatchewan association of rural municipalities convention that the government had a long term program. He referred to the resolution which he had introduced in this house with regard to land use, and spoke of the potentially great benefits which could flow from such a reform measure. While that may be true in principle, that is not what the government said it was going to do. It was not going to deal with the long term situation; it was going to embark on policies designed to meet the present plight of the Canadian farmer. Moreover, when the minister talked of this land use program he neglected to mention the foundation of that program which does not reside with this government. The basis of the bill which will ultimately be presented to this house, lies in the work of a committee sitting in the other place, as well as the representations which were made on at least two occasions by the federation of agriculture, these representations went so far as to provide the minister with a model bill, suitable for introduction, in respect of the development of agricultural land in our country in a productive way so as to enhance the income position of Canadian farmers.
But this measure, which is not even to be passed this session according to the announcement made by the minister when he introduced the resolution, can hardly be referred to as representing an agricultural policy. Certainly, it is not designed to meet the present plight of the Canadian farmer. I use the word "plight" advisedly, because if there was a plight when hon. gentlemen came into office the income position of farmers in Canada in 1960, 1959 and 1958 clearly establishes that there has been no improvement whatever in their situation. The minister cannot hope to give the impression in the country that because the government has this land use program in mind, such a program can serve as a substitute or as a means of covering up the lack now of a real agricultural policy for Canada. There is no such thing at the moment, notwithstanding what the minister may claim. There has been no over-all agricultural policy yet presented by this government to parliament which warrants the use of the phrase "over-all policy". Some of the objectives which such a policy might have were admirably stated by the present government when the Agricultural Stabilization Act was introduced. It is well for us to remember the general intentions which the government had in mind when it
Supply-Agriculture
introduced that measure. In the preamble to
that act we find the following:
Whereas it is expedient to enact a measure for the purpose of stabilizing the prices of agricultural commodities in order to assist the industry of agriculture to realize fair returns for its labour and investment, and to maintain a fair relationship between prices received by farmers and the costs of the goods and services that they buy, thus to provide farmers with a fair share of the national income-
As a statement of intention, that is an admirable statement, but the Minister of Agriculture is not going to persuade us that anything he has told this committee so far is in keeping with that objective or those intentions.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. I have to advise the hon. gentleman that his time has expired.

My estimates were introduced almost a month ago, and during that period I have been wondering just what the number two man in the Liberal opposition would have to say about them. All I can say at this time is that it is a good thing the bureau of statistics published this little pamphlet the other day to provide the hon. gentleman with a speech. There are a lot of things which can be done with figures, and I must congratulate the hon. member for Essex East on the efforts he has made this afternoon.
Before I go on to deal with some of the remarks he made, I should like to open my statement by expressing congratulations on behalf, I think, of all of us, to the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont who spoke last evening. I have been in this house for only a short time but one of the things which has struck me about the speeches made by representatives of the official opposition has been not only their lack of constructive criticism but also, and more alarmingly, their complete lack of awareness of the seriousness and complexity of the present farm problem. The hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont is a city member and does not pretend to be an expert on agriculture. Nevertheless, in his speech last night I found at least some evidence that someone in the official opposition was doing some thinking and trying to grope his way forward in the situation we have in Canada today. I believe the thanks of all Canadians should go to the hon. member.
Having said that I should now like to deal with the remarks of the number two man in the Liberal opposition who just resumed his seat. The figures quoted by the hon. member for Essex East were an attempt, in his usual facetious manner, to challenge the figures I gave when I introduced my estimates. In referring to my introductory remarks the hon.

Supply-Agriculture
member used such clear dramatic terms as "misconception" and said that I did not consider regions or commodities. The hon. gentleman said his figures were a direct contradiction of what I had said in the committee. These are abrupt and dramatic terms.
Let us take a look at the record and get out of the ether in which the hon. gentleman circulates. Let us examine what I did say. The hon. member said I did not consider the matter on the basis of region by region or commodity by commodity. I wish to direct the hon. member's attention to page 2406 of Hansard of February 24, 1961 where I am reported as having used these words:
I think it is necessary for me to point out that when one analyses the farm income of this country product by product and region by region, it soon becomes clear that the most variable area is the prairie province area.
I have said many times that the more one studies the statistics of farm income across Canada the more one realizes that there is inequality between regions and between commodities. This is one of the difficulties associated with being in a department where efforts are being made at long last to try to bring some stability to the industry.
Another remark made by the hon. member was that in my figures I had overlooked the transfer payments made by the government. I would direct the hon. member's attention and the attention of the committee to page 2405 of Hansard of February 24 where my introductory remarks appear. I quote now the eighth or ninth line from the top of the righthand column:
These figures give total cash income, which does include supplementary payments by the federal government.
I then went on to point out that this increased income was due to two factors, first the efforts of the government and, second, the efforts of the farmer himself. I also did something which the hon. member chooses to overlook. I gave the figures for the decline in the number of farmers in Canada for the last ten years. I could easily obtain these figures for the last 25 years.
This situation reflects the effort of the farmer to attempt to adjust himself to a revolution in agriculture both in terms of machinery and technology. As the farmer fights to make this adjustment the result is less farmers and more money per farmer. If you divide the fewer farmers into the greater amount of money naturally you get a greater income per farm.
I do not intend ever to boast about the fact that in the last three years there has been some little increase in farm income

because I, probably as well as any hon. member of the committee, know how far behind the farmer is in relation to comparable groups in the economy.
When I introduced my estimates I gave some indication of these small gains in the last three years. I do not think any hon. member of the opposition can escape the fact that in eaoh of the last three years the farm industry of this country has received, on the average, $351 million more than was received in the previous four years. I do not think that any hon. gentleman in the opposition can get away from the fact that the average income per farm in the years 1953-57 was approximately $4,300 and in the last three years it has been running at better than $5,200. Using fairly accurate figures that represents an increase of $900.
What about the cost of production?

The hon. member interjects "What about the cost of production?" Let me come to that point in respect of net income. I was honest with the committee, Mr. Chairman. Not only did I compare gross income over the whole farm industry but I also compared the gross income farm by farm. I then went on to compare what really counts, what is left over after you deduct the expenses.
In my opening remarks on February 24, I said that the efforts of the government were to some extent being nullified by the increasing costs. The hon. member for Essex East quoted figures from indices of prices. Prices have gone up in the last few years. What the hon. member overlooked is that there are on this side of this committee a few of us who remember that these indices start from 100. When did they get to this figure of 242? I invite hon. members of the committee to ask themselves that question. Go back over the last 25 years and examine the rise in costs, then look at the rise in costs in the last three years.
I do not want to get into debate at this stage of the consideration of my estimates, but let us examine the cause of this situation. A part of this question has been sent to a standing committee for consideration. I simply say to the hon. member for Essex East that he must think, with his completely old-fashioned Liberal arrogance that all wisdom rests with the party that thought it had divine right to rule. The hon. member must not think that the rest of us have no brains nor should he continue to think that what is good for the Liberal party is good for Canada.
Hear, hear.
This is an old-fashioned dogma concerning which the Canadian people made their opinion clear in 1957 and even more clear in 1958.
Egotism unlimited.

I wish to tell my hon. friends in the Liberal party that they must not be guilty of thinking that the people have forgotten why the Liberals were thrown out of office in 1957. If my hon. friends ever want to return to the right of the Speaker in this chamber they will have to realize that they must learn humility. When I look at the speeches made by hon. members of the official opposition, both inside and outside this chamber, I can readily see that those hon. members are a long way from having acquired the humility and broadmindedness that one would expect would be learned by an opposition. Judging from the progress they have made in acquiring humility I suspect it will take them a dozen or 15 years to learn this characteristic. There will have to spring up in the Liberal ranks a new group that will blow out the dust from the attic of the Liberal party.
Let us talk about agriculture.

I will admit that there are hopeful signs of the type to which I referred. I thought I detected a hopeful sign in the speech made by the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont. I assume that there may be some hope to be found among these younger men.
The hon. member for Essex East says, "Let us talk about agriculture." I should like to touch upon a few points dealt with in the remarks made by the number one man of the official opposition in terms of agriculture, the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska, who is the official agricultural critic of the Liberal party.
A real expert.

I wonder how long the hon. gentleman will have to reside in Canada before he comes to the realization that the people of western Canada fought a long time for the Canadian wheat board. They are very proud of it. It is their board and they feel they have the right to criticize it. But when the official spokesman of the Liberal party on agriculture stands up in this chamber, as the hon. member did, and unjustly criticizes the wheat board, there will be an answer some day.
(Translation):

Mr. Chairman, I rise on a point of order. Following the statement just made by the Minister of Agriculture, I must say that I have never spoken against the
Supply-Agriculture
Canadian wheat board. Let the minister read again my statement. If he did not understand my remarks in French, he should read the English translation and he will see that I did not speak against the Canadian wheat board. If he prefers that I repeat what I said, I am willing to do so right now.

We have some difficulty ourselves in understanding your French.
(Text):
He is just political.

I think the hon. member's point is well taken. When I accused him of attacking the wheat board I should have produced evidence of his having done so. I am having the English translation of the hon. member's speech looked up and I will give the hon. member the gist of it.
The minister had better wait until he gets the text.

The hon.
member said that last fall the producers in eastern Canada were not able to get western oats.

On a point of order, when one hon. gentleman denies a statement, the hon. member who makes the charge is in duty bound to accept the word of the hon. member. The Minister of Agriculture had an opportunity to refer to the text, but what he is doing now is paraphrasing-again misleading the committee- what the hon. member said, and he knows that is contrary to our rules.

I have been able to get a copy of his speech and I shall read some extracts from the remarks of the hon. member. This is the type of thing that we have in the translation; I am not responsible for that:
What do they want to say? After the results achieved in farming in the last four years, the remarks of the new Minister of Agriculture today should amount to more than so much hot air.
Then, he went on to say:
I would now like to address myself to the situation of feed grain deliveries in the eastern areas during the summer, until the closing of navigation. We learned in the newspapers that from August to the end of the navigation season, in the harbours of Montreal, Quebec city, Baie Comeau and others, a number of ships were waiting in line for two, three and even four weeks in front of elevators full of grain, particularly wheat for export. Those ships could not unload their cargoes, and there was no feed grain on the eastern markets.
In the meantime, our farmers were having all sorts of difficulties in getting supplies, and when they could get them they had to pay a high premium. Now, this shortage of feed grain on the eastern markets, was due to a decision of the Canadian wheat board to ship only export

Supply-Agriculture
grades to eastern ports. Incredible losses of the order of $1,000 to $3,000 were daily suffered by ship owners, not to mention the loss suffered by farmers who saw their operating costs increase on account of the higher prices they had to pay for their feed grain.
This certainly does not support what the minister has been saying.
There you have it, the number two expert backs up the number one expert on this statement.

On a point of order, the hon. gentleman is transgressing the rules of the house. He is now saying that I, too, have taken a position which supports his view as to what was said. In the statement that he has read he has clearly established that the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska did not take issue with the institution of the wheat board, and the play upon words by the Minister of Agriculture is such that the Chair must call the minister to order.
Oh, oh.

If I may be allowed to continue, in the face of the tremendous strength behind the ministry, I would say that the minister has no warrant whatsoever for saying that the words he has quoted justify the conclusion that the hon. member drew. The hon. member for Drum-mond-Arthabaska was seeking to explain a particular situation, and he was not attacking the wheat board. The Minister of Agriculture knows that full well.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I think it is a matter of interpretation of words. Both hon. members have made their points clear. Will the minister continue with his remarks.
I gather from your ruling, sir, that I am to be allowed to answer the point originally raised by the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska.
Provided that the minister keeps within the rules.
He is doing it; he is one of the few who do.

One thing I have learned in my short experience in the house is that you never know you have reached rock bottom until you see the suckers jump and squirm.
The statement I was objecting to was this:
Now, this shortage of feed grain on the eastern markets, was due to a decision of the Canadian wheat board to ship only export grades to eastern ports.
First of all, let me make it clear that the Canadian wheat board brings grain only to
(Mr. Hamilton (Qu'Appelle).]
Fort William and Port Arthur. The grain east of Fort William and Port Arthur is handled by the private grain trade and the big cooperatives in Quebec. If the big co-operatives in the province of Quebec and the private grain trade want to buy oats, they put an order in at Fort William and Port Arthur and it is moved east by the buyers. What actually happened last year was that the private grain trade and the co-operatives did not order in time to meet their commitments. As we were moving grain through to take advantage of the market that occurred for durum wheat in Italy, they brought their orders forward and it was impossible to fill them. As a result there was a delay of one or two weeks. The minute those orders were brought forward, we cleaned out the elevators and put in the grain.
This is not the only statement the hon. member made. I am still using the translation at the back of Hansard of February 24, where the following appears:
Because of the lack of Interest shown by the Canadian wheat board and the government, the eastern farmers will have to pay $300 more per carload for moving their grain than it would have cost them if that grain had been moved by ship at the proper time.
If this is not an attack on the wheat board, backed up by the number two man, the hon. member for Essex East, I do not know what it is.
The hon. member for Essex East asked me to speak about agriculture. I should like to say something that is reasonably positive in regard to this point because I know the situation in which the eastern farmers found themselves. I know how they were gouged by the dealers because of that temporary shortage. I have asked the wheat pools of the west to join with the Canadian wheat board in holding a meeting with the private grain trade and the big co-operatives of the east to see whether we cannot go out and show the eastern farmers that if they buy their oats in bulk in plenty of time in August or September for next year's supply- this is the time when they know what their own crops will be and what the supply picture will be in western Canada-they can save 10 cents a bushel. In other words, instead of paying 96 cents they will pay 85 cents if they buy in advance. This difference will pay for their storage. I should like to see a positive type of program which will benefit not only the eastern but the western farmer at the same time. The western farmer will get the same price and the eastern farmer will get his grain at least 10 cents a bushel cheaper. This is the type of positive proposal that I should like to put forward to meet this situation.
My time is about up, and I wish to conclude with this one observation. The hon. member

for Essex East keeps pontificating with the remark, taken entirely from his own imagination, that the agricultural program will not be passed this session.
The minister said so.

This indicates how clearly and slowly I must speak so that the number two expert of the Liberal party will understand. I asked the house for permission, after I get first reading, to stand the bill over for a period to allow me to consult with the farm organizations and the 10 provincial governments to see whether the bill would meet what they think would be best for all concerned. The hon. member makes a big play over the fact that I have asked that the legislation be held over until I can consult those organizations. I know from past experience that the previous administration never thought of consulting anybody, and that includes the farm organizations. They thought that they were destined to rule by divine right and were unconscious of the needs of farmers. They did not even bother to ask for the opinions of these organizations at all. We like to discuss some of these problems with farm organizations and with other governments. But this is a difference in philosophy which comes only through the humility of long years in opposition, which I hope the opposition will achieve some day.

I do not want to do an injustice to my hon. friend. If I have misinterpreted my hon. friend's intention respecting this legislation-and his words were open to that interpretation-I want to correct it. The federation of agriculture apparently thought likewise. Has the bill been referred to every provincial government and to every farm organization? When may we expect the reintroduction of the measure, and can the minister definitely say it will be introduced this session?

The resolution has been introduced; it has been debated in the house. The bill has not had first reading and, therefore, obviously I could not show it to the governments or to the farm organizations. The resolution is before the house. When first reading has been given to the bill I will be in a position to take it up with the provincial governments and farm organizations.
I want to conclude with the answer to a question I have heard repeated over and over again by the official opposition and, unfortunately, by the hon. member for Maison-neuve-Rosemont last night. I suppose if you hear something repeated often enough it almost becomes the truth, but the fact is that
Supply-Agriculture
back in 1958 after several months of hard work we came forward in the house with a national agricultural policy which the Prime Minister announced on August 30 of that year. We have been following that policy step by step ever since. We have brought legislation forward, put it on the statute books, set up the machinery and have been trying to work out the troubles that arise in the case of any legislation which produced those results which I have already outlined.
I should like to outline to hon. members just what that agriculture policy is. First and foremost, with 30 per cent of our agricultural production going into the export market we have to sell and sell. The hon. member for Essex East has difficulty understanding why, even though there has been a slight decline in prices during the last few years, the farmers are getting more money. One reason is that we are selling more units of these particular articles. I point this out because my colleague, the former minister of trade and commerce and now Minister of Veterans Affairs, caused many very competent farm leaders to scoff when he predicted in 1957 that he would go out and sell 300 million bushels of wheat a year. In the three years since, I think the average has been about 297 million compared with an average of 272 million over the previous ten years or the previous four years.
When I took over the portfolio of agriculture, and also responsibility for the wheat board, I set myself the same objective. I can now tell hon. members that not only is the figure of 300 million, which was set as a target by my colleague, going to be achieved in this crop year but, it will be met for a four year average. A lot more is going to be achieved by way of sales.
I do not want to repeat at this time what I said in Saskatoon on Wednesday when dealing with the outlook for agricultural products in western Canada but every farmer in eastern Canada knows it is in his interests that western farmers, who have to sell mainly in export markets, should be able to sell their products in order to keep the pressure off the eastern farmer in his home markets. I think there is no question of a clash between the two. It is a question of realizing their points of "complementarity".
Let me go on to the next point. I am not going to say that cash advances are a fundamental point of our policy. They were very useful in that they gave the farmer a chance to obtain an advance on the wheat he had produced until it could be sold. It does not cost the farmer anything and it helps to stabilize the economy from the point of view of income.

Supply-Agriculture
The first big item of the national agricultural program was the Agricultural Stabilization Act. It has been in effect now for three years and so far as the nine mandatory products and eight named products are concerned I think in most cases it is working fairly well. In my opinion prices have been stabilized and we are using the legislation wherever we can to raise prices slightly. We have had great difficulties, of course, with hogs and eggs and the technique we had to use over a year ago of changing from a purchase system to one of deficiency payments can only be described as Draconian. It was a very difficult decision to have to make. I think my predecessor as minister of agriculture, now Minister of National Defence, deserves the thanks of the people of Canada for having the courage to make that decision. It has enabled us to get rid of the very burdensome surpluses and to stabilize prices. I think we can go on now to the next step of looking at the legislation so far as hogs and eggs are concerned very carefully and seeing if we cannot make improvements that will achieve the objectives of the government, namely, the stabilizing of prices and also the bringing about of increased returns for those products sold within Canada. This may mean possible amendments to the act. I have asked the advisory committee to the stabilization board to look at two or three of these proposals this year so that next winter we can make up our minds finally as to what we are going to do about these two products.
I would think that all farmers in Canada will support the principles erf the act and will support any government that is willing to be open-minded, look at the facts as they are and see what it can do to make the act work. I do not have to tell the farm members of the house what a difference there is today. When you go to bed at night on the farm you know that if there is a sudden drop in world or domestic prices of the products you are producing you are not going to lose everything. There is a mandatory floor on the mandatory products and there are forward or support prices on all the products. It is a good act and I think we can make it work.
The next point in the national agricultural program is that enabling crop insurance legislation. At the present time only one province has a plan in operation but five other provinces are now working on plans. Active consideration is being given by us to at least two such plans. I predict that many of our specialty crops, and certainly our great cereal crops, will be under crop insurance in the very near future. There will be certain areas,

of course, which can never come under crop insurance because of their poor production. In other words, if the land is very poor and failures are frequent the rates would be so high that it would be impossible to bring such areas under the plan.
The big gun in the arsenal, of course, is the farm credit plan. If you can stabilize prices, if you can stabilize income, it is easier to work out a plan with the farmer that not only enables him to pay back the amount of money he has borrowed but also increases his income. I should like to remind my hon. friends opposite, without any maliciousness whatever, that when farm credit was under the Department of Finance, which has a different philosophy from the Department of Agriculture, loans to farmers across Canada amounted to approximately $8 million in a typical year. In some years it was lower and in one year the figure rose to $12 million, but $8 million is the figure for a typical year. In the first nine months that the farm credit corporation was operated under the Department of Agriculture loans amounted to $56 million, and by the end of the fiscal year the figure will be close to $60 million. According to the estimate for next year, the amount will be $75 million. When you go from $8 million to $75 million there must be a considerable difference in the philosophy and the difference simply is that the Department of Agriculture is actively and aggressively trying to help the farmers to get a plan that will improve their farm income as well as enable them to pay back their loans.
And also because there is greater need.

The need has been there ever since the 30's. We had farm loan acts during the 30's that were good starts but since the war they could not meet the tremendous capital costs required to run a modern, efficient farm. The farm credit corporation is still not perfect. I think there are at least one or two loopholes. There is a weakness in that it does not meet the conditions under which the maritime farmer must operate. There is a weakness in that it does not meet the needs of young lads who have no father to help them and have not got 25 per cent of the assets required. Weaknesses of this type must be apparent. This is the type of constructive criticism that I would welcome from the opposition because I am looking for answers to these problems. The advisory committee to the farm credit corporation, which committee is composed of representatives of farm organizations, is also looking into these problems. I do have some ideas and I would welcome

ideas from anybody because this matter is so important to the farmers that no question of politics should enter into it. It is a matter of a business arrangement. We turn down one out of every four farmers on the ground that they do not meet the requirements.
I see my time is up so I will conclude with one sentence. The other parts of the program involve conservation and of course, the rehabilitation plan. I do think that if you look at every other country of the world you will not find any country that has thought through its agricultural difficulties any better than we have or has come forward with such a coherent and logical plan.

Mr. Chairman, in opening my few remarks I should like to make reference to the suggestion of the Minister of Agriculture that there are certain ways by which parties become humble. If that is true I would suggest that we in this corner have simply gobs of humility which we are very willing to dispense to our friends at the left.
In presenting the views of this group I would be the first to admit that I myself am not a farmer. However, I would suggest that I have spent more time studying conceivable answers to the farmers' problems than on any other subject in the few weeks I have been in this house, and for that reason I do have a considerable amount of sympathy for the Minister of Agriculture. I think it is quite ironic when we turn to the estimates of the Department of Agriculture that we should be expected to look back into the past and expected to look at a sector of the economy which would be expressing something of an age that has gone. Yet, strangely enough, we are very much looking into the future. Although agriculture is becoming less and less the most important segment of our economy the effects of automation, and all the effects of the twentieth century, virtually are having more effect on agriculture than on any other sector of our economy.
In other words, the whole emphasis is that we have more and more production from a fewer number of people. Strangely enough man's output in the field of agriculture has gone up three times more than the output in manufacturing areas. I think this is one of the most serious problems which the Minister of Agriculture faces and suggests the tale of the sorcerer's apprentice who wanted to use the magical powers of his master to direct the broom to carry the water. Unfortunately of course, he could not stop the process and very soon would drown. We are being drowned in much the same way by the surpluses of our agricultural products to the extent that we have now 10 per cent less income going to farmers, according to the Manitoba farmers
Supply-Agriculture
union, than 10 years ago. We have 10,000 people leaving farms and where do these people go? Today the farms and cities have become more integrated. More and more farmers are sending their sons into the city. Unfortunately, because they have less seniority and are less trained to deal with the new technological age, they find themselves standing outside of the unemployment insurance offices.
A great deal of the difficulty in terms of unemployment relates back to this problem regarding agriculture. Indeed, around every city there are a great many people who are actually subsidizing their farming operation by working in manufacturing areas. You have men who are in a sense doing part-time farming and going into the city, taking a job away from someone else who has no other form of support, and then returning to work the farm. These individuals actually spend the money they earn in the cities in an attempt to keep the farm operating. That is the position to which agriculture has come; a very sorry state indeed in the 1960's.
As one drives through various parts of the country one sees abandoned farms. Certainly, in parts of eastern Ontario more and more farms are being sold for tax arrears. This, in itself, indicates the very sorry state of our agricultural community. I think we have learned that we cannot have a healthy economy in any country without a healthy agricultural economy. We learned this lesson during the 1930's when we found that our manufacturing and secondary industries were in very bad shape simply because we had not kept up our agricultural economy during this period but had let it fall behind in its purchasing power. As a result, the economy began to slow down. Now, the farmer produces even more than he did before. Perhaps because he is less organized or perhaps because he is less concentrated in his displeasure, his problems tend to be ignored. We are still I think concentrating on the wrong aspect of our agricultural problem. We are still concentrating on productivity.
I would suggest to the minister that more emphasis, both in our agricultural economy and in terms of the whole emphasis in the Department of Agriculture, should be upon marketing rather than upon productivity. This very much corresponds to the overemphasis perhaps of the government in other sections of our economy, such as the setting up of the productivity council when we really need a distributing council to distribute the goods of our nation in some just and sensible manner. I would hope that over a period of time we could take a look at some process for bringing these marketing boards together so that we can see the entire pattern of our

Supply-Agriculture
agricultural economy. I hope that the emphasis will constantly be placed, by the Department of Agriculture, on a process that will bolster and support all these pressures toward integrating these marketing boards.
I was surprised to find that in 1951, 58 cents of the Canadian dollar spent on agricultural products returned to the farmer and in 1956 only 44 cents of the dollar spent for food went back to the farmer. I think it is unfortunate if this trend continues. We must emphasize the need to have more of the dollar spent by the consumer returned to the hands of the farmer. I would suggest also that more emphasis must be placed on the securing of markets, both in terms of education and in terms of actual policy. I would certainly suggest that this is a great need in this country today. I think historians will find it strange, looking back on the twentieth century, to find that two thirds of the people of the world were going to bed hungry every night-as the hon. member for Greenwood mentions quite often and rightly so-yet surpluses existed in other countries which could not be used. I do not think historians, in looking back at the twentieth century, will say that we could not control our scientists but that we could not combine our surplus of food and the surplus of hunger in other parts of the world. I am sure that they will look with amazement at our agricultural policy in Canada and our attempt to cut down these surplus areas.
I am sure that this agricultural problem is one that must be solved especially in view of the fact that as scientists tell us, we will face difficulty in supporting the number of people that will be living on this earth in the next 50 or 60 years. We have not developed many solutions to these problems, but I am sure that is the aim of us all. I would certainly accept the fact that the Minister of Agriculture is attempting to find solutions. It certainly is the aim of the group in this corner to find a means of assuring that the farmers will receive their a fair share of the national income. Perhaps we might disagree as to what a fair share is, but they should receive a fair share of the national income. This share must be determined having regard to the family farm. I think the farmer has a right to expect that the economic unit which he respects will receive respect also from the government.
The only way we can really deal with this difficulty is to attack it directly with this in mind. I am convinced that the many direct plans, such as the resolution the minister has introduced to this house, are all to the good but at the present time price represents the main problem. It seems to me that transfer payments could be made to farmers with a

greater degree of efficiency than by simply allowing the farmer to go to the city to collect unemployment insurance, while at the same time he is unable to pay his taxes. He is, in effect, taking his portion of this $2 million being payed to the unemployed in Canada. Surely, some system of deficiency payment based on the cost of production and the number of units of production on a farm, no matter what the farm is producing, could be devised. That is perhaps the fairest and most efficient way of transferring this money so that it will bolster the farm economy.
I view with considerable interest the fact that the Minister of Agriculture has been travelling about the country and that also he has enlarged his public relations division in the Department of Agriculture. I think this is extremely important too. But I hope he is just not going around talking to farmers. I think the main problem which the Department of Agriculture must overcome is the rather mistaken belief that support prices, subsidies and deficiency payments are some form of glorious charity on the part of the rest of the people of Canada to the people who are seemingly unfortunate enough to be farmers. It appears that no one seems to recognize that tariffs and the cost of transportation into mining or forest areas are also out of the public purse and indeed right out of the pockets of the people of Canada, and that this cost is also a subsidy, although I wish we could get rid of that word entirely when we come to talk about means of bolstering the various sectors in our economy. But I think we need a full scale public relations job done to convince the people of Canada that although the number of farmers is becoming smaller, none the less they should receive as much concern and as much monetary support as do the other parts of our economy.
I think that surely more than anything else we have to find methods of distributing this large farm surplus we have on our hands. We have heard that the Department of Agriculture is determined to help the unemployment situation by distributing some of these farm surpluses to those who are unemployed. I sincerely hope that this will be done immediately. I hope that some sort of food stamp plan can be initiated in order to help the unemployed not three years from now, not six months from now, but in the very near future.
I would also suggest that the Department of Agriculture make every effort to enlarge the amount of food that is being given to other nations of the world. In that way the Department of Agriculture could greatly support the Department of External Affairs and extend its influence in world affairs. This would be to our advantage, because as the

other countries of the world become more and more able to buy, they will buy wheat instead of rice. They will be able to buy the high quality and high grade products which Canada produces in such large surplus. I can only hope that the Minister of Agriculture is using his influence to ensure that the tariff policies will not be to the detriment of the agriculture community. We listened with interest to the Minister of Finance when he told us that the legislation is not going to change the tariff policies of the Canadian nation. I hope not because if they are changed, and if we have a high tariff policy the people who will suffer, if they are not suffering sufficiently now, will be the farmers.
I hope the Minister of Agriculture will make every effort to make sure that the Canadian producer captures as much as possible of the domestic market. The Minister of Trade and Commerce has said a great deal about buying Canadian. I think this matter is just as important in the area of agriculture as it is in the area of secondary manufacturing. Perhaps it would help a great deal if agricultural products could be stamped or by some means identified as Canadian. I would hope that the Minister of Agriculture would solve this problem of identification of Canadian products so that people walking into a store will know that these food products are Canadian and will be able to encourage their local supermarket or grocery store to buy food products which will support Canadian farmers.
While there are a number of special areas in which the minister certainly will be taking an interest, the dairy farmers of Ontario have a number of problems to face. The farmers that I meet are particularly concerned about the fact that they sell their milk to the producer on the basis of manufactured milk prices and then find that this milk is used in various other areas which, of course, results in far greater profits to those who are manufacturing the milk. If this is untrue, I should be very happy to take this information back to my constituents. Unfortunately, this is certainly the feeling of those who are engaged in dairy farming in my particular part of Ontario. I am informed this is one of the reasons for the huge butter surplus, namely that the milk producers are using surplus milk in order to produce butter. Indeed, there is some fear on the part of these farmers that this prospective drop of 10 cents in the price of butter will have a serious effect on dairy farming in this particular area.
I was particularly shocked at the suggestion by one of the hon. members to the left that there should be two ministers of agriculture, one for the west and one for the east. It would seem to me, Mr. Chairman, if I may make the
Supply-Agriculture
suggestion, that what is needed more and more is greater integration of the problems of the western farmer and the eastern farmer. Heaven help us, let us not have two department's going off on separate tangents, neither taking into their complete consideration the problems of the other sector of the economy.
The farmers in eastern Canada I think are as much concerned as are the farmers in western Canada with regard to the weakening of the wheat board. The fear is, of course, that the cheaper grades of wheat will be fed to poultry and hogs in western Canada and this procedure will undercut the production in eastern Canada. That is a serious fear on the part of the farmers I have met. I sincerely hope that the minister will do everything in his power to make sure that these fears are unfounded and that the wheat board will continue to market wheat in an orderly fashion as has been done in the past in this nation.
We shall view with great interest indications that the Department of Agriculture will take a new and dynamic approach to the agricultural problems of this nation. We were heartened by the fact that the minister is concerned that farm prices will go up in the next ten years. May we only suggest that the time is now; that he might take the suggestion of the Department of Labour and adopt a do-it-now-attitude toward this problem, and that a far more dynamic approach might be taken towards giving our agricultural economy a healthy and prosperous basis on which to operate over the next number of years.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to take a few minutes to discuss the grant of $26,000 to the Agricultural Institute of Canada. I am one of the original members of this institute and am also fortunate in having a lifetime membership. I believe my hon. friend from Kootenay West is also a member of this institution and I know there are others in the House of Commons. This institute was organized in 1920. It was first called the Canadian society of technical agriculturalists. However, some few years ago the name was changed to that of Agricultural Institute of Canada. The figures that I obtained the other day indicate that the membership totals 3,065. These members are mostly graduates in agriculture from recognized universities. Members hold top scientific agricultural positions throughout Canada. I want to say that I know of no other group in the Dominion of Canada who are more dedicated to their work and to the advancement of agriculture than are the scientific agriculturists of Canada.
310E

Supp ly-A griculture
Our own deputy minister is a member of this society. The head offices are on Gloucester street. There are 32 branches of the institute: five in British Columbia, four in Alberta, six in Saskatchewan, three in Manitoba, seven in Ontario, three in Quebec and one in each of the other provinces of New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland. There is a national council, a president, a presidentelect and a vice president; there is an honorary secretary and a director from each province helping to run the business, and there are nine affiliated societies. Thus members can see that there are very few areas of a scientific agricultural nature which are not covered by this institution.
In what we term the hungry thirties this institute was operating, but with very little cash, and at that time the federal government gave grants to pay for the printing of the results produced by this scientific research into agricultural questions. The association did the experimenting and compiled the results; the government paid for the printing. This was the arrangement used to supply the public with the results of agricultural research in Canada. The grant now amounts to $26,000 and, I repeat, it is for the purpose of printing a scientific and economic review and other necessary papers and journals. The money is not used to support the actual work of the association but is merely in respect to the printing. The agricultural institute gets its revenue from its membership and from advertisements in different journals and papers.
I have here the November-December issue of the institute, Review. Hon. members will recognize the photograph on the front page. It is a photograph of one of the hon. gentlemen who spoke. I should like to put on record some of the items which are discussed in this particular issue. They include the Canadian Farm Building Plan Service, Rural Aging, Basic and Applied Research in Weed Control, the Inter-American Conference on Agriculture, expressions of opinion by recognized experts, and so on. These are some of the results published, and this is how they are printed. Often in days gone by we heard criticism of experimental and scientific research along these lines: This work is all done in institutions, but you do not get it out to the people who are interested in it. Well, this is the very thing that this agricultural institute does and I strongly support this grant of $26,000.
I do not want to sit down, Mr. Chairman, without saying that even though my constituency is 3,000 miles away from Ottawa I

have a couple of ladies in the gallery from the town of Chilliwack, one of the greatest places in British Columbia, and I am delighted to see them here.

As another charter member of the Agricultural Institute of Canada, and as a life member, I endorse wholeheartedly the speech which has just been concluded.

On a point of order, Mr. Chairman. We are being subjected to the trial of American firms; the hon. member has been discussing their case for at least ten minutes, and I should like him to revert to the matter under discussion.

If the hon. member will bear with me, he will see what I am leading up to, because I am conversant enough with the rules to know where I am going.
Just bear with me for a moment and you will see what I am leading to.

speechtext: Order. Perhaps the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska could tell us now what is the intent of his remarks so that we may decide whether they are relevant to the estimates now before us.

Mr. Chairman, the Canadian government granted patent rights to some firms which are now taking advantage of Canadian farmers with the levy of fees that we should not have to pay-and they achieve that through the use of a licence issued on December 2, 1958.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: So, as I understand, the hon. member wants to discuss the question of issuing a patent?

It is in direct relation with dairy products.
'Mr. Boulanger.]

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: For my part, I doubt that government policy with regard to issuing patents and trade marks, would be connected with the estimates of the Department of Agriculture, since the matter is under the jurisdiction of the Secretary of State.

On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, I think the point which the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska wants to make is that the attitude of those companies affects farm income, for he is trying to convince the house-and I am sure he will succeed-that dairy products are controlled by monopoly and that the farmers consequently are receiving less for their produce. I therefore think it is very appropriate to deal with this particular matter when discussing the agriculture estimates.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I may tell the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Racine) that he has been perhaps more convincing than his colleague, and if that is the intention of the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska, I shall allow him to continue his remarks. But, what the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska criticized earlier had to do with patents, which is not quite the same thing as a monopoly by some companies.
Just think of C. D. Howe. Big business indeed.

That is the present situation of the dairy industry. Therefore, I would ask the minister to inquire into the situation of those large companies trying to control the whole production and sale of milk powder in Canada.
We are demanding such an inquiry in order to know whether it is possible to remedy the situation before our farmers vanish from the scene at the rate at which they have been vanishing these last few years.
On behalf of the farmers of the province of Quebec and of Canada as a whole, we are asking that the support price of 64 cents a pound on butter, and of 32 cents a pound on cheese be maintained in Quebec, as well as in all the other provinces. At present, Quebec farmers are getting half a cent less a pound, so I would like the minister to tell us why they are not treated on an equal footing with farmers of the rest of the country.
We also urge the Minister of Agriculture to examine farming conditions in the east, and we invite him to come and visit the eastern part of the country. We read in the papers that the minister is always travelling in the west. So, we would ask him to come and visit the eastern farmers, those of the province of Quebec and of the maritimes, to realize what the actual situation is. Perhaps he will then be in a position to talk more often about it, when he takes the floor here to deal with agriculture.
