Mr. Chairman, in rising to participate for the first time in the discussion of the agriculture estimates I should first of all like to congratulate the Minister of Agriculture on his transfer to the department of which he is now minister. I say this because I personally feel he has brought to the department a knowledge that he has acquired through the years and an understanding of the problems of the farmers who are indebted to him for the many actions that have been taken.

Supply-Agriculture
I say this because only recently the Canadian Federation of Agriculture had a convention in this city and some of the delegates who attended that convention also took part in the mass march on Ottawa some time ago on which occasion we were given somewhat a rough time. However, these same people today want me to express to the Minister of Agriculture their feelings of confidence that he will do much for them and that he can display an understanding which was so lacking under the Liberal administration. If I may be permitted to make a comparison, they felt like delinquent children for many years and now they have found an understanding parent.
Perhaps the best thing that could be done so far as the Liberal party is concerned is to ignore the criticisms that have been levelled from that quarter. However, because there may be some people in the country who in a moment of weakness may feel that the Liberal party may have something to offer to them at some time in the future-certainly they did not in the past-I should like to refer to some of the remarks made by the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska. I am not sure whether he is the number one man or the number two man. When he first spoke on the estimates of the department on February 24 he said, as found on the first page of the English translation for that date:
__the farmers are losing confidence in their
government and, what is more serious still, are losing confidence in their profession.
I should just like to say that if anybody is losing confidence, whether it be a farmer or a businessman, and he feels that the profession he is following has no future, does he take out a loan? Does he go into debt? Certainly I would think that he would withdraw all his equity and run. This is definitely not the case with agriculture and I should like to compare the amount of loans in three years to show whether there is lack of confidence. From April 26, 1956, to March, 1957 loans amounted to $13,978,000. In 1957-58 the figure was $21,278,000 and in 1958-59 it was $30,145,000. Under the farm credit corporation, from April, 1959, to October 5, 1959, loans amounted to $23,215,000 and the figure for the period from October 5, 1959, to January 31, 1961, is $72,200,000. To me that certainly does not indicate a lack of confidence either in the way the government is administering the department or in the profession of farming itself. It is an indication that the farmers have renewed hope.

The hon. member continued to be critical of the government and said that it had channelled a lot of the taxpayers' money into agriculture. As found on page 2 of the English translation for February 24 he had this to say:
As a matter of fact, the cost to the Canadian taxpayers for meeting the commitments under the farm legislation was $77 million in 1960, $22.1 million in 1959 and $60.1 million in 1958.
He made a similar comment in participating in the debate last year. As found on page one of the English translation for March 25, 1960, he had this to say:
Under the Liberal administration, from 1946 to March, 1957, the Agricultural Prices Stabilization Act cost $25,052,806.98. Now if you look at the expenditures for the past three years, that is since the Conservative government took over, you find that in 1958 Canada spent close to $6 million and in 1959 $15,124,000. Now, for the year 1959-60 we are asked to vote $57,661,176.
That means that since the election of the Conservative government it has cost the taxpayers the substantial amount of $78,773,819 to support agricultural prices. In short, therefore, it can be said that in the last 12 years of Liberal administration it cost us $25 million to support those prices, while in three years of Conservative administration the amount expended was $78 million.
I have no apology for what the Conservative government has done. In his statement the other day the hon. member went on to say:
When will it put back in each farmer's pocket the $120 that the Liberal government took from him in taxes each year?
He is complaining that this government is putting back into the pockets of the farmers some of the money that the Liberal government had taken from them and, incidentally, the farmers too are taxpayers. It is no wonder that farmers today are looking forward to the present government carrying on in the manner it has. They well remember the $600 million that the British wheat agreement cost them. It will be a long time before they will look at anything that the Liberals have to offer.
The hon. member went off into the wilderness and ended up in a swamp when he tackled the question of the wheat board. I think the Minister of Agriculture dealt with that point and I will not deal with it further. The hon. member then went off on another tangent and decided to deal with the feed mill problem. I will be very brief on this point. The minister has put on record a table which indicates that prices are not depressed, as C.C.F. spokesmen would have us believe.
I should also like to point out that when the national farmers union presented their brief

this year they were critical of the new feed mill regulations. At that time I asked Mr. Atkinson, the vice-president of the Saskatchewan farmers union, why they should be critical since in their brief they thought that co-operatives should be expanded. I asked him why he should be critical since it appeared to me that the feed mill policy would be of direct assistance in the expansion of cooperatives. It certainly seems to me that would be the case in an area where a feed mill exists and the farmers are being paid lower prices. It seems to me that under those circumstances farmers should group together to form a co-operative and pay the price that the Canadian wheat board pays. This would certainly eliminate the existing feed mills. These farmers could establish themselves as supporters of the Canadian wheat board and could pay, as I have said, the prices the wheat board offers but at the same time abide by its regulations. I do not think this would hamper the development of cooperatives.
I asked him what he thought of this suggestion but his only reply was "I will see you later". I have neither seen nor heard anything from him regarding the problem as I presented it at that time but, I should like to know what his opinion is. I have written several letters pointing out my solution to this problem but have yet to receive a reply.
One other point I should like to mention is that farmers have for years been able to arrange deals among themselves and with others who were interested in paying a price for grain. During all the years I have been buying grain I have always had to pay a price if not equivalent to that offered by the Canadian wheat board, certainly higher. I do not understand why a farmer should allow himself to be taken in, if that is what is happening, because he has no obligation to sell his product.
The wheat board regulations were criticized and it was said the wheat board would be ruined if there were sales over and above the quotas. Anyone familiar with the situation will realize that there are special quotas for barley for malting purposes as well as special quotas for specialty oats and they have not ruined the wheat board. This situation has been in existence for many years. I do not intend to review it again now.
The next point I should like to bring to your attention, Mr. Chairman, has no reference to feed mills. Incidentally, the hon. member for Assiniboia said that the feed mill issue was the hottest issue today and he was sure that the government would have
Supply-Agriculture
to do something about it. This is the master mariner from the prairie who appears to have all the problems in hand, and claims that he can guide us over all sorts of troubled waters. I realize however that he has made mistakes before. He tried to take credit the other day for the big wheat sales to China and Czechoslovakia but I am afraid I cannot see that he had anything to do with them. However, if he wishes to take credit he must also accept the responsibility for the lack of sales under the Liberal government. He cannot have it both ways.
I should like in the little time left at my disposal to deal with a problem that vexes many farmers, and if I may be permitted I wish to follow my notes a little closer. I want to refer to the issue of permit books to producers. Each producer has one permit book in which are recorded all acreages leased. This creates a problem when a cash advance is required by the producer. In many cases the landlord resides miles away from the farm and in some cases out of the country. Before an advance can be obtained the landlord must sign a declaration. It is often impossible to get this declaration and the producer is then deprived of a cash advance. I have known of cases where the landlords simply refused to sign declarations, even though they might reside in the vicinity of the farms. I think this problem can be solved by having two permit books. One could be known as a producer's permit book and the other, perhaps, as the landlord's book. Each could be distinguishable by different coloured pages.
To illustrate what I have in mind, let us take the case of a producer who owns land of which 400 acres is cultivated and also rents land of which there are 300 acres cultivated. The basis of the rental agreement is, one third of the crop going to the landlord and two thirds to the renter. The producer, who is also a renter, would then be able to deliver on 400 of his own acres plus two thirds of the 300 acres making a total of 600 acres. The producer's permit book would then indicate that delivery could be made on 600 acres, while the landlord's book would register an acreage of one third of the total 300 acres or 100 acres on which delivery could be made. This would in no way mean that there would be any additional grain delivered as the total cultivated acreage is the same. The initial quota would, however, have to be divided on the basis of the agreement, even though the producer would have more of his own acreage. In other words, 200 bushels to the producer and 100 bushels to the landlord.
To take the same example, but in this case the rental agreement on a 50-50 basis, the renter would then have an acreage registered

Supply-Agriculture
in his permit book on which he could make delivery of 400 acres of his own land plus one half of the rented land, or a total of 550 acres. The landlord's book would in this case register an acreage of 150 acres. The initial quota would then be 150 bushels to the producer and 150 bushels to the landloard.
The situation becomes somewhat more involved when a producer rents land from several landlords. The same procedure is followed in calculating the acreage for the producer and the landlord, however, depending on the rental arrangement. The landlord and the producer would have to sign a declaration in all cases where the agreement is verbal before a permit book could be issued. If a rental agreement could be produced, an affidavit signed by the producer would be acceptable.
The objection could be raised that the initial quota, where the producer normally sells his own grain to meet his own expenses, would be small when it is split up between the landlord and the renter. This objection could be overcome by the fact that the producer could obtain a cash advance, and also by inaugurating a system whereby the landlords would be prohibited from making delivery until the first quota became available. Under this system it would also be possible for the landlord to obtain a cash advance. All such advances would be recorded and registered against this land, the owner of the land being responsible for the repayment, even if a transfer of land is involved. The onus for repayment always must remain with the owner.
This system would have the added advantage of removing the complaint of the landlords, in many cases older, retired people, that they are often not given a chance to sell grain because the renter supplies his own needs first by selling his own grain and thus fills the quota. This is not, of course, the concern of the government, but it would have the effect of correcting the situation.
I should like to make another recommendation to the minister regarding the proposed changes in the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act regulations. At the present time the Department of Agriculture allows a payment for the construction of dugouts to the extent of $250. This has been a good program in the past and has met certain needs of the farmer, but I suggest that it is perhaps time to have another look at the situation. The water that was stored in these dugouts certainly was not of the best quality. Very often it became polluted in which case it was not fit for human consumption. My suggestion to the department is that when a farmer undertakes to drill a well the department assume a portion of the cost equivalent to the cost of a dugout, providing the farmer can show

the department that there exists an adequate and good supply of water. In other words, if the department pays $250 toward the construction of a dugout for water it is only reasonable to suggest that the department should now pay the same $250 toward the drilling of a well. This would work in conjunction with the new program being undertaken by the department, and I am of course referring to the rural development program.
The other suggestion I wish to make is one which should meet with the approval of the hon. member from Assiniboia. As reported at page 2413 of Hansard of February 24, he said this:
I was, of course, for many years a sharp critic of Mr. Gardiner because the average prices established under this legislation were not payable as some of us felt they should be directly to the producer, or they were not guaranteed to the producer. Instead, they were paid to the packing company and the farmer had to deal with the packing companies and do what he could to get from them the established floor.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR NATIONAL FLAG, ANTHEM AND INDEPENDENCE DAY
PROVISION FOR NATIONAL FLAG, ANTHEM AND INDEPENDENCE DAY
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-22 respecting the sovereignty of Canada.
(Translation):
He said: Mr. Speaker, this bill deals with the expression of the sovereignty of our great country. Throughout its history, Canada has known a constant constitutional development and has become a sovereign state within the commonwealth of nations.
A state is sovereign when it enjoys supreme authority in its own territory and is subordinate to no other state in the international field. Sovereign does not mean absolute, since all states must submit to public international law.
It can be proudly stated that our country enjoys today the eight main attributes of a sovereign state. These are the right to legislate; the right to make our legislation extraterritorial; the right of diplomatic representation abroad; the right to have Canadian courts of last resort; the right to declare peace; war or neutrality; the right to amend our constitution as we see fit; the right to negotiate and to ratify ourselves our own treaties; and finally the acknowledgment of our sovereignty by the other countries of the world.
Many factors and events have brought about the realization of this maturity. But the most outstanding was the Statute of Westminster, passed on December 11, 1931, and granting our country its sovereignty and independence within the commonwealth.

It is not enough to enjoy Canadian sovereignty that is so often referred to in this house, at the United Nations, in NATO, and everywhere else throughout the world. That actual sovereignty must be reflected by external signs that would proclaim our distinctive Canadian personality.
This national need to express ourselves in a distinctive manner is not in any way detrimental to our relations with other commonwealth members to whom we are united by our common allegiance to the crown.
Mr. Speaker, it is mainly this spirit that motivates the introduction of my bill the reminder of an existent Canadian sovereignty and, as external signs to express it: a distinctive national flag, a distinctive national anthem, and a national sovereignty day.
I realize that this government faces a number of economic problems. However, the bill that I have the honour of introducing is not unrelated to the success of our efforts in all fields. In fact, the achievement of these three objects will promote understanding between Canadians from coast to coast, show that Canadian patriotism is really alive and stir up a national dynamism, likely to increase the efforts required for the development of our great country.
In the course of these remarks, we will deal separately with the first two objects of the bill, although the reasons which commend them to us are practically the same. But a common aspect which should be pointed out immediately has to do with the interpretation of the term "distinctive". Both instances involve the adoption of a flag and of an anthem that distinguish and characterize our national colours and our national aspirations, and that differ from designs or anthems of all other countries.
It is not the first time that this matter comes up in the political forum of Canada. In the past, governments, associations, members and many Canadians have raised this important issue, without getting any definite results.
The status quo of flags in Canada seems to be as follows: from 1760 to 1892, we hoist the union jack and the red ensign. In 1892, Sir John Macdonald, in an effort of national development, is granted the use of the red ensign, with the arms of Canada reproduced in its field, for merchant vessels registered in Canada. In 1911, the union jack is indicated as being our statutory flag to be flown officially over land in Canada. In 1924, use of the red ensign is authorized on all buildings which the Canadian government owns or occupies abroad. On September 5, 1945, the

late Mackenzie King adopts an order in council which imposes the red ensign as the Canadian flag, with the arms of Canada in the fly and the union jack in the upper part, and that until parliament decides otherwise.
Considering the origin and the history of flags, we find that the union jack remains the national emblem of Great Britain, under a royal proclamation of January 1, 1801, and that the red ensign, authorized in England by Queen Anne in 1707 and by Queen Victoria in 1864, constitutes, under section 72 of the Merchant Shipping Act of 1894, the national flag for all vessels and boats owned by British subjects.
Now, if Canadians really wish to demonstrate the new Canadian citizenship which has been theirs since January 1, 1947, and if those same Canadians want to display a distinctive patriotism, those two flags are no longer suitable as legitimate expressions of their feelings. Besides, the order in council of September 5, 1945 does state that the red ensign will be flown until parliament decides otherwise. That order in council recognizes a temporary situation which we must now correct by something definite, by the adoption of a distinctive national flag for our own Canada.
Since the last war, Canadian opinion in this field has steadily developed and it has now attained a degree of maturity which leaves no cause for doubt.
Why has the time come to act? Because our country needs external signs of its legal and progressive sovereignty. Sir Robert Borden signed, on behalf of this country, the peace treaty of Versailles. In 1923, Mr. Ernest Lapointe signed in Washington what was the first official treaty negotiated by our nation with a foreign country without recourse to the services of a representative of the London government. On December 11, 1931, under the Bennett government, the Statute of Westminster recognized the independence and the sovereignty of our country within the commonwealth. During the last war, Canada was the first country in America to declare war on Germany. Later on, the federal government appointed a Canadian to the position of governor general. Appeals to the privy council of England were abolished and, as I was saying, a Canadian citizenship established on January 1, 1947.
In the field of external affairs, Canada has shown itself to be a distinct power in the military as well as in the economic field. Must we recall its membership as a 90205-6-197

distinct nation in the United Nations, in the Colombo plan, in NATO and within the disarmament committee of ten nations. It has more and more ambassadors and plenipotentiary ministers throughout the world.
The world is learning to appreciate our initiative and our mediation. Such an important situation must not be jeopardized by the absence of a flag. We would otherwise expose ourselves to unfortunate incidents such as Nasser's protestations during the Suez crisis of 1956. Let us recall that the United Nations police force then responsible for the maintenance of peace in Egypt included men from Canada, Colombia, Denmark, Norway, Pakistan and Sweden. All those countries but Canada had a national flag, a distinctive flag.
If our country has grown up so much and if that evident maturity is acknowledged from every quarter, we should then exteriorize that emancipation through a really Canadian and truly distinctive national flag. The pride and future of our country is at stake. Most Canadians have a keen desire to live not for countries where their distant forefathers were born, but for the land which feeds them and will finally receive them.
Such a flag will strengthen the convictions which were at the origin of the confederation of 1867. It will materialize our common aspirations, our parliamentary and individual freedoms, our national understanding and our Canadian patriotism.
The various political parties represented in the federal parliament have already indicated a clear stand in favour of the adoption of a distinctive national flag. Resolutions along those lines were unanimously adopted by the Conservatives at their convention in December 1956, and by the Liberals at their rallies in January 1958 and January 1960. On November 8, 1945, as shown on page 1939 of Hansard, the C.C.F. leader, Mr. Coldwell, had this to say:
I wish to see Canada with a distinctive flag, and in my opinion the red ensign with our coat of arms on it, which I would rather say nothing about, is not a distinctive flag.
Now, if all Canadians need such a flag, if they ask for it in such a way with the support of political parties, if the international community sees in us a child who has reached maturity and his distinctive personality, what are we waiting for? I have every reason to believe this proposal will be welcome and that the house will soon give it the stamp of its approval.

Private Bills
If we adopted a distinctive national flag, we should at the same time have to designate a distinctive national anthem. Because, how could we salute our own flag while singing the national anthem of another country? It would be absolute nonsense.
There is no longer any doubt that our country has reached maturity and that it intends to develop along that line. In 1958, Mr. Vincent Massey, our past governor general, acknowledged this national awareness. This is what he said then:
X feel that we have learned to he Independent and proud of our country. We shall retain our identity as long as we remain true to our traditions while showing our independence.
For many years, two anthems have been sung in Canada-the one entitled "O Canada" was composed by a Canadian; the other, the royal anthem is "God Save the Queen".
For the reasons given above, it is essential that we now select a distinctive national anthem, i.e. an anthem likely to satisfy the aspirations of the greatest number of Canadians and one that would not be the national anthem of another country, by its origin, its composition and its expression.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the "God Save the Queen" that we admire and like to sing on various occasions, is recognized as the national anthem of a friendly country, Great Britain. By its origin, its composition and its expression, it does not reflect the Canadian spirit.
As a matter of fact, "God Save the Queen" has various origins and a European past. History reports that when the French King Louis XIV entered the chapel of Saint-Cyr, the boarders broke into that song, the words of which had been written by the superior, Madame de Brinon, and the music composed by Jean-Baptiste Lully.
Grand Dieu, sauvez le roi,
Grand Dieu, vengez le roi,
Vive le roi!
Que toujours glorieux,
Louis victorieux,
Voit & ses pieds ses ennemis Toujours soumis!
According to tradition, Handel, the famous German composer, patronized by the king of England, visited Saint-Cyr in 1721, obtained permission to transcribe the song, translated it into English and offered it to King George I. Later, the song was slightly changed and became England's majestic "God Save the King".
Some authors have it that the melody of "God Save the King" was at some time or

other, with appropriate words, of course, the national anthem of Prussia, Germany, Switzerland, and even Russia.
All this shows that "God Save the Queen" is deeply rooted in history. It has been the national anthem of England since practically the year 1745, during the Scottish revolution.
But there is nothing typically Canadian about it. That is why time has come to add to a distinctive Canadian flag a national anthem which will stir up the emotions and the feelings of Canadians.
As a third external sign of Canadian sovereignty, the bill proposes a national sovereignty day which would be celebrated each year on December 11, to commemorate the Statute of Westminster.
We must not be afraid to stimulate pride and patriotism in Canada. We must give to all Canadians an opportunity of becoming more aware of our constitutional development, and to express their joy of being Canadians, with all the advantages inherent in Canadian citizenship.
The annual observance of a national holiday would provide this opportunity and special celebrations in the various provinces and in the schools would further stimulate Canadian patriotism among our young people.
In ancient times, people worked hard at inculcating love of country in the minds of the young. Thus, in Athens, the young ephebus, that is the young Greek between 18 and 20 years old, went up on the Acropolis to swear allegiance on his honour to his country.
Such a ceremony could be revived on independence day if young Canadians were invited to take an oath and to pledge themselves to the service of our great country.
Mr. Speaker, before concluding may I be permitted to state the substance of the bill which it is my privilege to submit:
The healthy instinct of independence of a nation is anchored in the hearts of its people. Although certain historical traditions may, for a time, restrict that instinct it cannot be expected that it will be dormant eternally. Any nation with pride in its achievements in peace and war and conscious of its own sovereignty will insist that its status be recognized by other independent nations.
A distinctive national flag, a distinctive national anthem and a national independence day constitute external signs of sovereignty and it is the purpose of this bill to provide these three worthy attributes for our country.
Thus:
Whereas since the 11th of December, 1931 Canada is a sovereign nation, among the members of the commonwealth of nations, with them united by

a common allegiance to the crown, equal in status and in no way subordinate to the United Kingdom;
Whereas the sovereignty of Canada should be made evident by the adoption of a distinctive national flag, the designation of a distinctive national anthem and the observance of a legal holiday on the 11th day of December in each and every year;
Therefore, Her Majesty, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate and House of Commons of Canada, enacts as follows:
1. This act may be cited as the National Sovereignty Act.
2.	Canada is hereby declared to be a sovereign nation.
3.	It shall be the duty of the Canada council to prepare or have prepared, after competition or otherwise, a design for a suitable distinctive national flag free of the emblem or emblems of any other country and to submit the same to the Senate and the House of Commons of Canada within one year of the coming into force of this act.
4.	Notwithstanding any royal prerogative and anything contained in any act, of the parliament of the United Kingdom such design for a national flag, after it has been approved by a joint resolution of the Senate and House of Commons, shall be submitted for approval to Her Majesty the Queen and for the issuance of a royal proclamation under the great seal of Canada respecting such ensign, armorial flags and banners as Her Majesty shall be pleased to appoint.
5.	It shall be the duty of the Canada council to select after competition a distinctive national anthem for Canada and to submit the same to the Senate and House of Commons of Canada within one year from the coming into force of this act.
6.	The anthem mentioned in the previous section shall become the national anthem for Canada after it has been approved by a joint resolution of the Senate and House of Commons of Canada.
7.	Throughout Canada, in each and every year, the eleventh day of December (not being a Sunday) , being the anniversary of the day the Statute of Westminster, 1931 was assented to, shall be a legal holiday and shall be kept and observed as such, under the name of Canadian independence day.
8.	When the eleventh day of December is a Sunday, the twelfth day of December shall be, in lieu thereof, throughout Canada, a legal holiday, and shall be kept and observed as such under the same name.

However, I do not wish to go on record without mentioning the 22 years of discussion on a distinctive Canadian flag, which did not produce a legislation providing for such a distinctive national flag. But I can say, as the hon. member for Sherbrooke mentioned in his remarks, that in the past several members have proposed legislation about a distinctive national flag.
Many are inclined to believe that when a member introduces a private bill and a discussion is started on that bill it is a waste of time for the House of Commons.
Such opinion is erroneous. On the contrary, I feel that every time matters as important as a national flag, a national anthem and a national independence day are raised in this house, we contribute through discussions as objective as the one just proposed by the hon. member for Sherbrooke, to mould public opinion in our country.
If we did not adopt a flag under the former regime-and I am not alone in deploring the fact, it is deplored by all members-the reason is, in my humble opinion, and the former prime minister indicated it repeatedly, that a flag must be a symbol of unity for all the citizens of a country.
He undoubtedly felt, because he was aware of it, that the public opinion was not ready to adopt a distinctive national flag.
In fact, every Canadian is free and everyone has a right to his own ideas about a distinctive national flag.
We should not criticize those who do not think as we do. On the contrary, we must try

Private Bills
to make them understand our point of view that in an independent country, in a country which has therefore reached maturity in all fields, it is a duty and a right to think of a distinctive flag which will reflect our history, aspirations and independence.
So, I entirely concur in the proposals of the hon. member for Sherbrooke who has put in quite a different way remarks which we have been hearing here for any years.
About the flag, I recall that some 15 years ago, while I was in Ethiopia, in the heart of dark Africa, to teach geography, those young Ethiopians-I am glad to pay tribute to their emperor-were born with the love of their parents' country in their hearts.
And those pupils could not understand that a country like Canada, of which so much is said around the world and which has earned the sympathy and esteem of all other countries, did not have its own distinctive flag.
I used to explain to them what I just told the house, that public opinion was not ready for it yet. But they had a question which almost forced me to silence: "But do not all Canadians have for their country the same love as we have for ours?"
The question, we must admit, was too difficult for me to answer and too difficult for them to understand.
So, I want to say to the hon. member for Sherbrooke, who has introduced this bill, that we are all in favour of a distinctive national flag.
I would even say that the people of Canada are becoming more and more in favour of distinctive national flag.
About a year ago, I was reading in an important magazine that a poll has been conducted among students in the 15 to 21 age group in most high schools and other schools in this country. The results of this poll showed that 70 per cent of our young people are in favour of a distinctive national flag.
I think, Mr. Speaker, this poll showed a very interesting change in Canadian opinion.
With regard to the national anthem, I think there has been less progress than in the case of a distinctive national flag. However, I am pleased that it has been included in this bill and I hope the demand for a truly Canadian national anthem will increase.
Of course, that does not keep us from singing "God Save the Queen", whenever the occasion arises, singing it with all our heart

and soul. But it would also be appropriate to sing a song of devotion to our country and to our forbearers.
Unfortunately, I think it will take a few years more before we get practical results, namely a truly distinctive national anthem.
Like the hon. member for Sherbrooke, hon. members will have to raise the matter often in their constituencies, with children and students and in discussions with their colleagues.
There will probably have to be many speeches made on the matter of a distinctive national anthem, but I am confident we will get it; I am even confident that we will get it before I draw my old age security pension.
With regard to the suggestion of a Canadian independence day, it becomes a corollary, as was so well shown by the hon. member for Sherbrooke, to the matter of a distinctive national flag and of a distinctive national anthem.
I do not want to take up any more of the time of the house. In closing, may I again commend the hon. member for Sherbrooke who has shown remarkable objectivity in launching the discussion of the bill.
Such speeches can only draw the various elements of our population closer together; they can only create mutual sympathy between the two groups composing it.
As the hon. member for Sherbrooke had set the tone of this discussion of his bill, I felt I had a duty to follow his example and express my views, in the hope that others would do the same.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I too wish to join the hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Brassard) in congratulating the sponsor of the bill, the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Allard). His address to the house was logical and sincere and I would say it had some merit in it. However, I wish to depict the other side of the coin. There are always two sides to every question. I think that when both hon. members who preceded me expressed the view that all Canadians want this and want that, they were taking a lot for granted because all Canadians do not want the flag they have in mind, do not want to change the national anthem, do not want to discard July 1 as our national holiday and replace to with December 11. Therefore when they say that all Canadians want these things they are stretching matters too far.

Private Bills
This is not the first time we have discussed this subject. It has come up before. Certainly, it comes before us in different forms. The wording of the bill or resolution is slightly different but the intention and object are the same, namely, a distinctive Canadian flag. This matter is a perennial one and, in fact, comes before the house almost monthly. I have no objection to that. In a democracy we are free to discuss both sides of a problem. I am not going to say that all Canadians agree with me but I know a lot of Canadians who do and I am going to quote a few of them today.
I have spoken on this subject before and to summarize my stand it is simply this. I am in complete accord with legislation being passed to bring about a distinctive Canadian flag but somewhere on the field of that flag I want the union jack. There are thousands and millions of people who support me in that view and that can easily be proved. I dread this controversy, but maybe it is all to the good. I am sorry that there are some people whose only mission in life appears to be to go down in history as having sponsored something altogether different.
I am glad that the hon. member for Sherbrooke did not say what some have said in the house, that they are ashamed of the flag we have, the red ensign; that they are embarrassed every time they look at it; that it hurts their national pride; that it is a symbol of servitude and colonialism; that it is a foreign emblem and so on. I am glad that the hon. member for Sherbrooke, as I understood his remarks, did not use any of those terms because I and thousands and millions like me are not ashamed. We are not embarrassed. We do not consider the union jack an emblem of a foreign country. There are many thousands and millions in this country who still consider that island as the old land and who feel they are going home when they visit that country.
Those of my race have certain attachments to that flag and that is why we would like to see it appear on any new Canadian flag. We would like to see some portion of any such flag allocated to the union jack because we are proud of it and are proud to live under it.
The bill before us probably goes further than any other measure we have had before the house. We have discussed a flag before but this bill seeks to bring about a new national anthem. Do hon. members suffer any indignation or shame when they sing "God Save the Queen", or is this a step in trying to break
away from the mother of parliaments, from the Queen, from the monarchy to which we are so attached?
The bill also provides for a new national holiday. What is wrong with July 1 which we now observe as our national holiday? What is wrong with that? Should we break all ties with the past; forget sovereignty, forget our heritage and our ancestry? No one is asking us to do that in Canada today. We are attached to the crown, and we in Canada are proud to say "God Save the Queen".
This bill envisages that the government or parliament will legislate and declare this and this to be the national anthem. Are we going to prohibit everybody from singing "God Save the Queen"? These I suggest are probably the first steps to be taken in that direction, like the first steps taken by the people of South Africa. This bill proposes that we rid ourselves of this, and this, and finally do away with everything represented by British justice and everything for which British fair play stands. It is suggested that we have something completely new.
I feel I am echoing the feelings of many people in Canada. I am just as sincere in my thinking as I presume the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Allard) was in his. I do not doubt his sincerity. I feel that he is honest and means well, but does he suggest that we break away completely from everything in the past? If that is what he means I would ask him why we should then adhere to any of our traditions. I cannot for the life of me understand why some people question the existence of our sovereignty, and suggest only that we have an invisible connection with it. What is sovereignty? I have checked the meaning of this word in several dictionaries and find the best definition contained in volume 25 of the "Encyclopaedia Americana". The definition given there is as follows:
In political science the supreme power in a state by which the government is administered.
Further on in that definition we find the following statement:
-the people were the ultimate source of political authority and the same principle was advanced by the French revolution.
I do not understand those people who say that since we have no flag of our own we have no full sovereignty. The hon. member for Sherbrooke discussed this subject in some detail, but I intend to go just a step further. There is not a single foreign soldier on Canadian soil except those who are here with the permission of the government of this country. I suggest that we are completely independent.

speechtext:
The hon. member now says let us show it. I would suggest to him that we show it by our actions. I should like those individuals who feel we have no sovereignty to visit the iron curtain countries. Let them take a look at the situation in the satellites. Those hon. members who have been fortunate enough to visit the United Nations have seen what those countries regard as their representatives to the United Nations, and I speak of countries such as Poland, Czechoslovakia, Bulgaria, Romania and the like. Do these representatives act independently at the United Nations? No, they most certainly do not. I will go even further than that and mention the land of my fathers, the Ukraine and its neighbour Byelorussia. They are members of the United Nations but the foreign ministers, as we know them, of the Ukraine and Byelorussia have never appointed one single representative. They have yet to appoint an ambassador or even open an office in other nations. This is what I call a state without sovereignty.
We certainly have control over our own external and domestic affairs and everyone knows it. A statement to the contrary would cause the horses out west to laugh, and we do not intend to do that. We have representatives at the United Nations and ambassadors in many other countries of the world. Surely, no one could say that our Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker), who played such a leading and brilliant role at the prime ministers' commonwealth conference in London just a few days ago, was not the representative of a country with sovereignty. There certainly does exist evidence by which all those peoples of the world know that we are a sovereign nation and I would suggest that those individuals who think otherwise are blind. Surely we do not want to be placed in the position the peoples of South Africa find themselves in today. I am sure they will regret that they entrusted their affairs of state to individuals like their prime minister.
Where is the servitude and imperialism that we have heard about in this house? We have heard that "God Save the Queen" is a foreign anthem. That national anthem is not the anthem of a foreign nation, it is an anthem which we sing because we consider the queen to be the head of our state, and we revere Her Majesty Queen Elizabeth II as our queen. The hon. member for Sherbrooke asks us to insult her by proposing in this bill that she approve a different flag. Everyone realizes that we have had 2,400 different designs submitted, and

I am sure we will receive 2,400 more. We would be asking Her Majesty to approve a new national anthem and I would suggest that we might receive 2,400 different versions of it.
As I have suggested before, it is impossible to legislate what exists in the hearts of the people; that which lives there must grow there.
I realize, Mr. Speaker, my time is running out but I must suggest that those individuals who propose that we discard our flag, our national anthem, and even our national holiday are proposing something which will not be received by the people of Canada. This proposal suggests we abandon our celebration of July 1, the date of the formation of our dominion. I am sure that the people of Canada will not accept such a suggestion. In this connection I should like to quote a portion of an article written by Peter Dempson, a gentleman of some reputation in our press gallery, in the Brandon Sun. Part of that article reads as follows:
The choice isn't likely to be a surprise. It will probably be the Canadian ensign, the flag that was flown over most federal government buildings since 1924, and under which our armed forces fought in world war II and the Korean war.
I would be interested in knowing who could mistake those forces as the forces of some other country than Canada.
Mr. Dempson states further in his article:
Canada really doesn't need a flag more distinctive than the Canadian ensign. It's known the world over as Canada's flag. It's raised aloft whenever a Canadian or a group of Canadians is being honoured.
Surely this type of statement does not suggest that Canadians want something that has no connection at all with our past and no connection at all with the union jack. I could quote further, Mr. Speaker. With your permission I wish to refer to Torch, the magazine of ex-service men and women. That organization is a large one. You are taking a great deal for granted when you say that all Canadians want something. These men fought under that flag. Here is what they did in 1960 at Windsor. It is interesting to note that the Canadian Legion is pressing for this change.

Torch "The Voice of the 'Corps' ", states as follows:
At their 1960 dominion convention in Windsor in June they passed a resolution (this was the first time they had formally made reference to the matter) strongly urging the Canadian government to pass an act confirming an order in council of September 5, 1945, which declared the Canadian red ensign to be our national flag.
That comes from men and women who fought under this flag. Mr. Speaker, I am going to ask your permission to let me quote another part of Mr. Dempson's article which is under the heading "The Flag that Stands on Guard". He states as follows:
Recognition in the form of federal legislation isn't really necessary to make the Canadian ensign our flag, for in every sense it is our flag, but to make the whole thing official, the government could introduce legislation spelling out the Canadian ensign as our national flag.
I hope the government does that. I hope so for the simple reason that it would end all controversy, and all these endless debates on a matter upon which we differ. That is true enough.
Mr. Speaker, I can quote individuals. I have received a large number of letters. One out of 25 did not agree with me when I spoke on this question in 1959. I admit that.
Business of the House
However, Mr. Speaker, my opinion is that as long as the people of Canada who are sovereign, who are independent and who are building up a Canadian race-it is true it is on the basis of two basic races- allow anything to disrupt their unity they are not doing this country a favour. My feeling is this. Canadians are not unanimous on this subject. Those that say they are unanimous are just as far off the beam as I would be if I said that. As long as Canadians are so divided and as long as they are sincere, we as legislators cannot ram something down their throats. I agree with the hon. gentleman who preceded me when he said that these discussions are of benefit. They are helpful. But nevertheless they are creating public opinion. The time may come when Canadians will be unanimous, but today they are not unanimous.
I think I will just have time to quote one letter, Mr. Speaker. I have quoted the Legion. I am now quoting a letter from an individual. This book is full of these letters. Any hon. member who wants to see them is welcome to do so. Addresses and, in some cases, even telephone numbers are given. This letter is from St. Mary's of the River, Fredericton, New Brunswick, is dated June 6, 1959, and is addressed to me at the House of Commons, Ottawa. It reads as follows:
Dear Mr. Mandziuk:
Congratulations upon your speech in the house about the flag.
I have a dear friend of Polish birth who feels the same as you do and for the same reasons.
You can do a great deal of good making new Canadians realize that what they value in Canada was created by Britain.
That is under the union jack, and that letter is signed by Mrs. E. W. Sansom. I could read others.

Question
The following answer, deposited with the Clerk of the house, is printed in the official report of debates pursuant to standing order 39:

1.	What is the cost to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation of the current series of the 90-minute "Festival 61" T.V. play?
2.	Who were the people responsible for buying this particular program?
3.	For how long is this program contracted for?
Answer by: Hon. George C. Nowlan (Minister of National Revenue):
I am informed by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation as follows:
1.	The budgeted costs of productions in the current series "Festival 61" have varied between $14,000 and $65,000. The series has presented a number of different types of program, including opera, Shakespearean drama, modern drama, and musical programs. For example, some of the programs have been "H.M.S. Pinafore" presented by the Stratford festival company; a production of "Julius Caesar"; the drama "The Old Ladies"; and a program featuring the Canadian pianist Glen Gould. The costs have varied according to the different requirements of each production.
2.	The C.B.C. is responsible for the purchase of scripts and the production of all programs in the series.
3.	The series is scheduled throughout the current fall-winter season on a weekly basis.
